intuition: A permutation has the same character counts as the original string. Slide a window of exactly len(s1) characters across s2 and compare its counts with s1's counts. We do not need to generate any reordered strings to check whether a match exists.

Because the alphabet contains only 26 lowercase letters, a fixed count vector describes each signature. As the right boundary moves, increment the arriving letter. Once the window is full, decrement the letter that falls off the left, keeping exactly len(s1) positions represented.

A matching pair of vectors proves a permutation appears because every letter has the required occurrence count. Comparing 26 entries takes constant time per window. Sets would be insufficient: they cannot distinguish words such as aab and abb, whose distinct letters agree but counts differ.

steps: For s1="ab", target counts are one a and one b; the required window width is two.
Scanning s2="eidbaooo", the first complete window "ei" has different counts, so continue.
At right=2, add d and remove e, leaving "id". At right=3, add b and remove i, leaving "db"; neither matches.
At right=4, add a and remove d. The current window is "ba", with exactly one b and one a.
The two count vectors now agree, so return true immediately. Later o characters do not need to be examined.

concept.question: How can a fixed-size letter inventory recognize a rearrangement?
intuition: Generating every permutation of the query is unnecessary. Any rearrangement has exactly the same occurrence count for every letter and exactly the same length.
Slide a section of query length across the text while maintaining its letter counts. Compare its inventory with the query’s inventory. A matching inventory means that section is a permutation.
concept.observation: Both letter multiplicities and section length must match.
approach: Maintain text sections of exactly the query length.
Update leaving and entering counts and test for inventory equality.
concept.correctness: Two equal-length strings are permutations exactly when every letter count agrees. The sliding updates remove precisely the leaving character and add precisely the entering one, keeping each section’s inventory exact. Every possible start of a query-length section is checked, so a match is found if and only if one exists.

complexity.explanation: Counting and scanning are linear in the two text lengths. Inventory comparison uses the fixed 26-letter alphabet, so extra storage is constant.

pitfalls: Both letter multiplicities and section length must match.
A set of letters loses multiplicities: aab differs from abb.
